newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cocoa fad hits sweet spot for Japan confectioners.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa fad hits sweet spot for Japan confectioners.

text.p: A fad for cocoa drinks among young Japanese shows no sign of fading, and confectioners expect profits to stay at lipsmacking levels.
The sweet spot will likely be this winter, after a hot cocoa boom last winter that is thought to have lifted cocoa imports to record levels, traders say.

"Japan's manufacturers, anticipating good sales, have aggressively launched new cocoa products," one trade house source said. "Cocoa consumption could peak in January and February, when students prepare for entrance exams," he said.
Media reports in Japan late last year saying cocoa is high in fibre and helps relieve stress helped spark a hot cocoa boom that emptied supermarket shelves.
The boom motivated Japanese cocoa manufacturers to boost imports of both cocoa powder and beans, and to expand their domestic production capacity, including grinding facilities.

Japan's cocoa powder imports in the first seven months of calendar 1996 rose to 8,358 tonnes from 3,380 tonnes in the same period a year earlier, while cocoa bean imports rose to 32,753 tonnes from 24,661 tonnes, according to the latest Finance Ministry data.

Masahisa Uchino, director-general of the Chocolate & Cocoa Association of Japan, said he expected domestic output of cocoa powder, which is produced from beans, to at least double in calendar 1996 from last year's 2,568 tonnes.

A spokeswoman for Morinaga and Co Ltd, which holds more than a 50 percent share of Japan's cocoa drink market, said: "Even though sales of cocoa (for hot drinks) slowed in the summer off-season, our cocoa shipments this summer were believed to be three to four times those in summer 1995."

Morinaga has launched a new cocoa product for this winter season which it says dissolves more easily in hot water than existing products. It is also only mildly sweet, allowing consumers to add sugar to taste.

Some traders said Japan's retail sales of hot cocoa drinks could rise to around 35 billion yen ($318 million) this year from about 20.0 billion yen ($181 million) in 1995 and about 10.0 billion yen ($90.9 million) in 1994.

Looking to next year, although traders doubt the pace of last winter's boom can be sustained, they said there is still substantial room for growth as Japan's chocolate and hot cocoa consumption lags far behind other industrialised countries.
"Japan's retail hot cocoa sales are currently only about one-fifth those of instant coffee," the Morinaga spokeswoman said.
She added that sales this autumn and winter would be the key to whether hot cocoa would become an established part of everyday life for Japanese or whether it was really just a fad.

Traders also said that despite the sudden surge in hot cocoa's popularity, growth in chocolate consumption had remained sluggish, due partly to a spreading diet boom especially among young women. ($1=110 yen)
